```{r functions, echo=FALSE}
draw_half_court <- function() {
  court_theme <- theme_minimal() +
    theme(
      axis.title = element_blank(),
      axis.text = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks = element_blank(),
      panel.grid = element_blank()
    )
  
  court <- ggplot() +
    # Court elements
    geom_circle(aes(x0 = 0, y0 = 0, r = 7.5), color = "gray") +   # Rim area
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = -8, xmax = 8, ymin = 0, ymax = 19), fill = NA, color = "gray") + # Paint
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = -25, xmax = 25, ymin = -5, ymax = 47), fill = NA, color = "black") + # Court border
    geom_circle(aes(x0 = 0, y0 = 19, r = 6), color = "gray") + # Free throw
    geom_segment(aes(x = -22, y = 0, xend = -22, yend = 14), color = "gray") + # 3pt line
    geom_segment(aes(x = 22, y = 0, xend = 22, yend = 14), color = "gray") +
    geom_curve(aes(x = -22, y = 14, xend = 22, yend = 14),
               curvature = -1, color = "gray") +
    coord_fixed() +
    court_theme
  return(court)
}

draw_half_court_layers <- function() {
  list(
    geom_circle(aes(x0 = 0, y0 = 0, r = 7.5), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "gray"),   # Rim
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = -8, xmax = 8, ymin = 0, ymax = 19), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = NA, color = "gray"),  # Paint
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = -25, xmax = 25, ymin = -5, ymax = 47), inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = NA, color = "black"),  # Border
    geom_circle(aes(x0 = 0, y0 = 19, r = 6), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "gray"),  # Free throw
    geom_segment(aes(x = -22, y = 0, xend = -22, yend = 14), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "gray"),  # 3pt sides
    geom_segment(aes(x = 22, y = 0, xend = 22, yend = 14), inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "gray"),
    geom_curve(aes(x = -22, y = 14, xend = 22, yend = 14), inherit.aes = FALSE, curvature = -1, color = "gray"),  # 3pt arc
    coord_fixed(),
    theme_minimal() +
      theme(
        axis.title = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank()
      )
  )
}
```

## Overview

The NBA Cup is a recent addition to regular season play with a tournament debut in 2023. All NBA Cup games contribute to regular season records except the championship game.

The Bucks' 2024 NBA Cup championship game was played against a team who, in regular season, had the highest offensive and defensive rating in the NBA (compared to our no.11). OKC is a statistically sound team with superstars and MVP nominees like Shai Gilgeous-Alexander accompanied by a deep roster of heavy contributors. During there first match-up of the year, without doubt, the OKC Thunder were expected to walk away with a trophy. What circumstances fostered the Bucks' success in the NBA Cup finals?

This report addresses the five major findings from this game's data that led to our success:

1.  [Sticking to Our Strengths](#strengths)

2.  [Reliable Defense](#defense)

3.  [Randomness](#randomness)

4.  [Opponent Underperformance](#OU)

5.  [Unfamiliarity](#unfamiliarity)

```{r import data, include=FALSE}
shots <- read_csv("data_mil_okc_121724_shots(in).csv")
team_min <- read_csv("NBA_Cup_Minutes_Played - Sheet1.csv")

str(shots)
str(team_min)
```

## League-Wide Norms

```{r, echo=FALSE}
ggplot(shots, aes(x = factor(contestLevel, levels = c("uncontested", "lightly_contested", "heavily_contested")), 
                  y = qSQ)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of qSQ vs Defensive Contest",
       x = "Contest Level",
       y = "Quality Shot (qSQ)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r regression, echo=FALSE}
# Fit the regression model
nba_contest_model <- lm(qSQ ~ contestLevel, data = shots) 
pander(nba_contest_model)
```

The regression reveals a significant, negative relationship between variables; that across teams, as contest level goes up (i.e uncontested to heavily contested), the probability that a shot goes in goes down. These results are expected since tougher defenses across the NBA will produce lower scoring opportunities for opponents.

## Contributions to Our Success

### Sticking to Our Strengths {#strengths}

```{r shotsuccess, echo=FALSE}
sqvss <-shots %>%
  group_by(team_nba_off) %>%
  summarise(avg_qSQ = mean(qSQ, na.rm = TRUE),
            actual_fg_pct = sum(fg)/sum(fga)) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_qSQ)) 

kable(sqvss, col.names = c("Team", "Avg Shot Make Probability", "Actual FG Pct"))
```

At a very basic level, we can observe that under the same average shot difficulty, we put in more shots (42% efficiency compared to their 33%). The gap in actual field goal percentage could point to exceptional Bucks defense or cold shooting from OKC.

```{r, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
shots %>% 
  filter(team_nba_off %in% c("MIL", "OKC")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = complexShotType, fill = team_nba_off))+
  geom_bar( position = 'dodge')+
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("green", "blue"))+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

### Shot Distribution

#### Heat Map

```{r heat map, echo=FALSE}
shots %>%
  filter(team_nba_off %in% c("MIL", "OKC")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = loc_x, y = loc_y)) +
  geom_density_2d_filled(alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~team_nba_off) +
  draw_half_court_layers() +
  labs(title = "Shot Density: Bucks vs. OKC") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r bar plot, echo=FALSE}
shots %>% 
  filter(team_nba_off %in% c("MIL", "OKC")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = complexShotType, fill = team_nba_off))+
  geom_bar( position = 'dodge')+
  scale_fill_manual(values=c("forest green", "blue"))+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

From the heat map and bar chart, we can draw that OKC had greater diversity in their shot selection. However, we had noticeably higher catch and shoot makes, catch and shoots with relocation, stand-still layups, and tips. Both charts display the Bucks' ability to convert on shots near the rim and in their most effective corners.

#### Court Region and Shot Type

This chart displays the top 5 most effective shooting regions for each team

```{r, echo=FALSE}
top5_shots <- shots %>%
  group_by(team_nba_off, region) %>%
  summarise(
    fg_pct = sum(fg) / sum(fga),
    attempts = n(),
    .groups = 'drop'
  ) %>%
  filter(fg_pct > 0) %>%
  group_by(team_nba_off) %>%
  slice_max(fg_pct, n = 5) %>%
  arrange(team_nba_off, desc(fg_pct)) 


kable(top5_shots)
```

##### Bucks

**We were extremely effective from high-value zones,** (e.i., Left wing three, Right corner three, Restricted area). Our perimeter shooting is notably strong: we shot **85.7% from the left wing three** (6 of 7), and **57.1% from the right corner three** (4 of 7). Shooting well over league average.

##### OKC

OKC's **left corner two** was notably less effective (33.3%, 2 of 6). Mid-range zones such as the **left wing two** and **middle two** each returned **50% FG**, though on low volume (3 and 6 attempts respectively).

### Reliable Defense {#defense}

To understand whether the Bucks' defensive strategy made an impact, I next examined shot contest levels.

#### Defensive Contest

```{r tab-summary, echo=FALSE}
dc <- shots %>%
  group_by(contestLevel, team_nba_off) %>%
  summarise(fg_pct = sum(fg)/sum(fga),
            avg_qSQ = mean(qSQ, na.rm = TRUE),
            attempts = n()) %>%
  arrange(contestLevel)
kable(dc, col.names = c("Contest Level", "Team", "FG Pct", "Avg Shot Make Prob", "Attempts"))
```

##### Uncontested

OKC took slightly more difficult uncontested shots and were more efficient from them, meaning our defense likely slacked off due to the perceived low probability that a shot would go in.

##### Lightly Contested

Avg shot `qSQ` difficulty was comparable however, we converted at a much higher rate! Our ability to convert lightly contested shots at a higher rate could indicate superior shot selection and offensive execution.

OKC's low conversion on lightly contested shots point to a Bucks defense forcing OKC into shooting from tougher spots. This is confirmed in scoring and shooting performance by player table where we find starters like Shai with lower average`qSQ` or shot make probabilities.

##### Heavily Contested

The average shot difficulty `qSQ` was similar for both teams, OKC was able to achieve slightly better shooting performance in the presence of heavy defense. This points to a high defensive caliber of both teams; us matching the tenacity of OKC, the NBA's regular season leader in defensive rating, with our own resilient defense.

### Randomness {#randomness}

```{r, echo=FALSE}
defense_summary <- shots %>%
  group_by(team_nba_def) %>%
  summarize(
    opponent_fg_pct = mean(sum(fg)/sum(fga)),  # Averaging FGs when this team is defending
    avg_qSQ_against = mean(qSQ, na.rm = TRUE), # Average shot quality faced by this team's defense
    avg_contest_level = mean(as.numeric(factor(contestLevel, levels = c("uncontested", "lightly_contested", "highly_contested"))), na.rm = TRUE),
    attempts_faced = n(),    # Total attempts faced by the defense
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

kable(defense_summary, digits = 3, caption = "Defense Performance Summary by Team")
```

With similar average shot quality and contest level---both of which were uncharacteristic based on regular season data---and a higher volume of shot attempts, the evidence suggests that OKC was simply *unlucky*. The Bucks seemingly made more shots than expected against OKC, even though they didn't take higher-quality or less-contested ones.

#### Catch-and-shoot Effectiveness

```{r, echo=FALSE}
cse <- shots %>%
  filter(catchAndShoot == 1) %>% 
  group_by(team_nba_off) %>%
  summarise(fg_pct = sum(fg) / sum(fga),
            avg_qSQ = mean(qSQ, na.rm = TRUE),
            attempts = n())
kable(cse)
```

The similarity in average shot quality (MIL: 55.2, OKC: 55.4) indicates that both teams were generating similar quality of catch-and-shoot opportunities. The higher attempt rate signifies an successful game plan that created more opportunities through effective ball movement and off-ball player movement. The game strategy focused on leveraging catch-and-shoot opportunities contributed to greater scoring.

#### Assists and Passing

```{r, echo=FALSE}

assist_data <- shots %>%
  group_by(player_nba_passer, team_nba_off) %>%
  summarize(
    Assist_Opps = sum(assistOpp),
    Assisted_Shots = sum(assisted)
  ) %>%
  group_by(team_nba_off) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = Assisted_Shots, n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  arrange(team_nba_off, desc(Assisted_Shots))

knitr::kable(assist_data)
```

The assist data highlights contrasting offensive structures between us and OKC. For us, **Giannis** **clearly served as the offensive hub**, generating 19 assist opportunities, resulting in 10 assisted shots.

**OKC's playmaking was more distributed**, with Jalen Williams, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, and Isaiah Hartenstein each generating 7--8 assist opportunities, **though with fewer converted assists**. This spread suggests a **more balanced but less efficient** scheme in this matchup, contributing to their lower overall offensive efficiency.

### Opponent Underperformance {#OU}

#### Scoring and shooting performance by team

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Group by team and player, summarize shooting stats, then filter top 6 by FGA per team
shooting_data <- shots %>%
  group_by(team_nba_off, player_nba_shooter) %>%
  summarize(
    FGA = sum(fga),
    FG = sum(fg),
    FG_Percentage = FG / FGA,
    ThreePA = sum(fga3),
    ThreeP = sum(fg3),
    ThreeP_Percentage = sum(fg3)/sum(fga3),
    Avg_Distance = mean(distance, na.rm = TRUE),
    Avg_qSQ = mean(qSQ, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  group_by(team_nba_off) %>%
  slice_max(FGA, n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  arrange(team_nba_off, desc(FGA))

kable(shooting_data)
```

##### Bucks

Starters like Dame, Giannis and Brook maintained high `FG` and `ThreeP` percentages while steadily creating shots with low difficulty/ higher make probabilities.

Forwards like Prince creating shots with **higher make probabilities** and guards like Green and Trent Jr. shooting maintaining outstanding `ThreeP` efficiencies while creating shots with higher probabilities of makes, compared to starters like Dame, undoubtedly contributed to the team's success.

This table's outcomes show a successful game plan that prioritized player's strengths and set them up for success.

#### Shot Quality vs. Makes for starters and bench

```{r combineddata, include=FALSE}
#merging
team_min$MIN <- as.numeric(team_min$MIN, units = "mins")
team_min <- team_min %>%
  mutate(MIN = as.numeric(MIN) / 60)
team_min <- team_min %>%
  mutate(MIN = as.numeric(MIN) / 60)

# Merge datasets and calculate efficiency metrics
combined_data <- shots %>%
  left_join(select(team_min, Player, Team, MIN, STATUS), by = c("player_nba_shooter" = "Player", "team_nba_off" = "Team")) %>%
  group_by(player_nba_shooter, team_nba_off, STATUS) %>%
  summarize(
    Total_Points = sum((fg - fg3) * 2 + fg3 * 3),  
    Attempts = sum(fga),
    Minutes_Played = first(MIN),  # Picking minutes from `team_min`
    PPM = Total_Points / Minutes_Played,  # Points per minute
    FG_Percentage = Total_Points / Attempts
  ) %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  arrange(team_nba_off, desc(PPM))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
plot_1 <- ggplot(combined_data, aes(x = Minutes_Played, y = PPM, color = STATUS)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = player_nba_shooter), size = 3, max.overlaps = 10) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, color = 'gray') +
  facet_wrap(~ team_nba_off) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between Minutes Played and Points per Minute",
    x = "Minutes Played",
    y = "Points per Minute"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot_2 <-ggplot(combined_data, aes(x = Minutes_Played, y = FG_Percentage, color = STATUS)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = player_nba_shooter), size = 3, max.overlaps = 10) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE, color = 'gray') +
  facet_wrap(~ team_nba_off) +
  labs(
    title = "Minutes Played vs Field Goal Percentage",
    x = "Minutes Played",
    y = "Field Goal Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```

```{r side-by-side-plots, fig.width=14, fig.height=6, echo=FALSE, out.width='100%'}

(plot_1 | plot_2) + plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1))  # Ensure equal widths
```

Kenrich Williams, Ajay Mitchell, and Alex Caruso combined for 2 made field goals on 14 total attempts. With these role players underperforming, it reinforces the notion that OKC's offensive inefficiency in the game was more about underperformance.

In the midst of OKC's sub-optimal performance, we had **a bench who stepped up**. Players like Gary Trent Jr. and AJ Green outperformed most starters when accounting for the amount of minutes played.

## Key Takeaways

There are several factors that contributed to our NBA Cup Finals win. OKC is a team with a stacked roster of talent, favored highly on both offensive and defensive ends. Intuitively, there must be a *give and take* that allowed us to prevail given the circumstances. Here's what that looks like:

1.  [Sticking to Our Strengths]{.underline} - The Bucks benefitted from multiple contributors shooting well within their historical strengths. Brook Lopez and Damian Lillard each **shot 50% from three**. Notably, bench players like Gary Trent Jr. and Andre Jackson Jr. took shots with comparable or even *better* expected shot quality than some starters . This suggests **our game plan generated good looks for everyone.**

    Importantly, our bench did not take significantly lower-quality shots. Players like Andre Jackson Jr., Taurean Prince, and AJ Green had some of the **highest average shot quality** (e.g., Jackson Jr. at 60.6 qSQ, Prince at 60.4), and Green even shot 60% from the field. This suggests that our offensive distribution created good looks regardless of who was taking them.

2.  [Reliable Defense]{.underline} - Defense was instrumental in our victory. **We forced OKC to take tougher shots**. We maintained a consistent defensive effort, effectively contesting shots without sacrificing shot efficiency. The defensive contest levels revealed that while OKC had slightly better shooting performance on uncontested shots, **we grossly outperformed OKC in lightly contested shots**. Additionally, in heavily contested scenarios, both teams displayed similar defensive intensity, but the Bucks were able to limit OKC's high-quality scoring opportunities, contributing to their success.

3.  [Randomness]{.underline} - League-wide probabilities explain that there is a strong **negative** relationship between contest level and make probability; **with tougher defensive efforts, make probability should go down**. This was not the story for OKC's offense. The Bucks grossly outperformed OKC on lightly contested shots. Nearly a third of OKC's shot attempts where lightly contested yet converted only 18% of the time compared to our 52% for lightly contested. As such, the outcome of the game may reflect more randomness than entrenched competitive advantages.

4.  [Opponent Underperformance]{.underline} - OKC's primary scorers Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Jalen Williams combined for **44 FGA but converted just 16**, yielding a collective **FG% of \~36%**, well below regular season efficiency. Despite averaging decent quality shots (e.g., Shai's qSQ = 49.0), their actual shooting fell short of expectation. This underperformance, especially given the volume, significantly limited OKC's offensive output. Additionally, Isaiah Joe and Lu Dort, typically relied on for perimeter shooting, went **1-for-10 from three**, despite solid average shot quality (qSQ \> 50). These figures underscore not just tough shooting luck, but a failure to capitalize on decent opportunities.

5.  [Unfamiliarity]{.underline}{#unfamiliarity} - Finally, t's important to note that **the NBA Cup Final marked the first meeting between the Bucks and the Thunder this season**. Without prior head-to-head context, both teams entered the matchup without acquaintance or familiarity with each other's tendencies. This lack of previous exposure may have **amplified the role of variance in shooting outcomes and defensive matchups**.

The NBA cup final marked a career performance for many Bucks players in the face of a sub-optimal opponent performance. The well thought-out game plan that played to the strengths of each player and also forced opponents to play uncharacteristically contributed to our success in the NBA Cup Final.
